title: The birth-stories of Nanak
hookLine: janamsakhis are collections of Nanak's life-stories written down from the 1600s onward

lines: A BARGAIN, A RIVER, THE WRONG WAY.
cards: A boy sent to market with money and told to strike a good bargain, who comes home with empty hands. A young man who goes into a river and is given up for lost.
A traveler who lies down with his feet the wrong way and is scolded for it. Pictures like these are how some children first meet Guru Nanak. The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't tell these stories.
They come from old books of stories about his life. Today: the birth-stories of Nanak.

teach.b: Janam is birth. A sakhi is one story, one episode. Together they name a whole kind of book: the janamsakhi, a collection of sakhis about Guru Nanak's life, from his birth to his passing.

teach.h: THE GRANTH IS HYMNS, NOT A LIFE STORY.
teach.b: First thing to know: Guru Nanak's own words are in the Guru Granth Sahib, but that book is hymns, not biography.

So the stories of his childhood, his travels, his meetings with holy men and kings, come to us through tellers: Bhai Gurdas, whose vars we've just been reading, and the janamsakhis, written down after his lifetime, tradition says from what his Sikhs remembered and retold.
Second: there isn't one janamsakhi. There are several traditions of them, each with its own shape and its own tellers, and the same story can come out differently in each.
Over the next few days we'll meet them one at a time. Third, the heart of it: a janamsakhi isn't trying to be a modern biography, with checked dates and footnotes. It's devotional.
Each sakhi is told to carry something: a teaching about truth, about the Name, about who counts as holy. Some sakhis include miracles; others are plain and human.
Historians read them carefully, sorting what may be early memory from what grew later. Sikhs read them for what they teach, and some readers do both at once. Neither reading cancels the other.
So the line isn't stories that are facts.
It's stories that carry truth: a sakhi can be weighed by a historian and still carry something true to the listener.

how: Sikh families and gurdwara teachers retell sakhis of Guru Nanak from the janamsakhis, especially to children and on gurpurabs, as stories that carry the Guru's teaching.

o: a birth chart drawn up for a newborn
a hymn sung to celebrate a baby's birth
a book of stories of Guru Nanak's life

practice: Take one of the pictures from the start, the boy who came home from market with empty hands, or a short sakhi you know, and let it play once.
Don't ask yet whether it happened exactly that way; ask what it's carrying, what the story is trying to hand you, and let one answer come. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when it does.
